substances.name: semaglutide
substances.statement: In the EU, semaglutide is a centrally authorised prescription medicine: Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for weight management (EMA and HMA, June 2024).
substances.quote: The medicines Bydureon, Byetta, Lyxumia, Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity and Victoza are authorised for diabetes only. Saxenda and Wegovy are authorised for weight management and Mounjaro is authorised for both diabetes and weight management. All these medicines (called GLP-1 receptor agonists) are prescription medicines and should only be used under medical supervision.
substances.quoteEn: The medicines Bydureon, Byetta, Lyxumia, Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity and Victoza are authorised for diabetes only. Saxenda and Wegovy are authorised for weight management and Mounjaro is authorised for both diabetes and weight management. All these medicines (called GLP-1 receptor agonists) are prescription medicines and should only be used under medical supervision.

substances.name: semaglutide
substances.statement: In the EU, Ozempic (semaglutide) has held an EU-wide marketing authorisation since 8 February 2018 and is prescription-only (EMA).
substances.quote: Ozempic is available as a solution for injection in prefilled pens and can only be obtained with a prescription. … The European Commission granted a marketing authorisation valid throughout the European Union for Ozempic on 8 February 2018.
substances.quoteEn: Ozempic is available as a solution for injection in prefilled pens and can only be obtained with a prescription. … The European Commission granted a marketing authorisation valid throughout the European Union for Ozempic on 8 February 2018.

substances.name: semaglutide
substances.statement: In the EU, Wegovy (semaglutide) has held an EU-wide marketing authorisation for weight management since 6 January 2022 and is prescription-only (EMA).
substances.quote: Wegovy can only be obtained with a prescription. … Wegovy received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 6 January 2022.
substances.quoteEn: Wegovy can only be obtained with a prescription. … Wegovy received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 6 January 2022.

substances.name: semaglutide
substances.statement: EMA's safety committee concluded on 6 June 2025 that NAION, an eye condition that can cause loss of vision, is a very rare side effect of semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy), affecting up to 1 in 10,000 people.
substances.quote: PRAC has concluded that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide (meaning it may affect up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide).
substances.quoteEn: PRAC has concluded that NAION is a very rare side effect of semaglutide (meaning it may affect up to 1 in 10,000 people taking semaglutide).

substances.name: tirzepatide
substances.statement: In the EU, tirzepatide is authorised as Mounjaro (EU-wide authorisation 15 September 2022) for type 2 diabetes and adult weight management, prescription-only; no EU product named Zepbound was found in the Union Register or EMA data (searched 25 September 2026).
substances.quote: Mounjaro is also used together with diet and physical activity to help adults to lose weight and keep their weight under control. … Mounjaro can only be obtained with a prescription. … Mounjaro received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 15 September 2022.
substances.quoteEn: Mounjaro is also used together with diet and physical activity to help adults to lose weight and keep their weight under control. … Mounjaro can only be obtained with a prescription. … Mounjaro received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 15 September 2022.

substances.name: retatrutide
substances.statement: In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing retatrutide was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).
substances.quote: This includes information on marketing authorisations of centrally authorised medicines and post-authorisation procedures. … These pages also contain information on medicines for which the European Commission has refused a marketing authorisation, or has suspended or withdrawn the marketing authorisation after approval.

substances.name: afamelanotide
substances.statement: In the EU, afamelanotide (Scenesse implant) is authorised only for erythropoietic protoporphyria, under exceptional circumstances (European Commission, 22 December 2014), and is prescribed only by specialists in recognised EPP centres.
substances.quote: Scenesse is an implant used to treat patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare disease that causes intolerance to light. … Scenesse is only prescribed by specialist doctors in recognised centres for treating EPP and should only be used by doctors who have been properly trained. … Scenesse has been authorised under ‘exceptional circumstances’. … The European Commission granted a marketing authorisation valid throughout the European Union for Scenesse on 22 December 2014.
substances.quoteEn: Scenesse is an implant used to treat patients with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare disease that causes intolerance to light. … Scenesse is only prescribed by specialist doctors in recognised centres for treating EPP and should only be used by doctors who have been properly trained. … Scenesse has been authorised under ‘exceptional circumstances’. … The European Commission granted a marketing authorisation valid throughout the European Union for Scenesse on 22 December 2014.

substances.name: baricitinib
substances.statement: In the EU, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been centrally authorised since 13 February 2017; its indications include severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over, and it is prescription-only, started by a doctor experienced in the condition (EMA).
substances.quote: Olumiant can only be obtained with a prescription, and treatment must be started by a doctor who has experience in the diagnosis and treatment of the conditions for which it is used. … Olumiant received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 13 February 2017. … Baricitinib is indicated for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adult and adolescent patients 12 years of age and older.
substances.quoteEn: Olumiant can only be obtained with a prescription, and treatment must be started by a doctor who has experience in the diagnosis and treatment of the conditions for which it is used. … Olumiant received a marketing authorisation valid throughout the EU on 13 February 2017. … Baricitinib is indicated for the treatment of severe alopecia areata in adult and adolescent patients 12 years of age and older.

substances.name: baricitinib
substances.statement: Since EMA's January 2023 review, JAK inhibitors including Olumiant should be used in people aged 65 or over, at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk, or long-term smokers only if no suitable alternative exists, and this applies to alopecia areata.
substances.quote: These medicines should be used in the following patients only if no suitable treatment alternatives are available: those aged 65 years or above, those at increased risk of major cardiovascular problems (such as heart attack or stroke), those who smoke or have done so for a long time in the past and those at increased risk of cancer. … EMA has now concluded that these safety findings apply to all approved uses of JAK inhibitors in chronic inflammatory disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, ulcerative colitis, atopic dermatitis and alopecia areata).
substances.quoteEn: These medicines should be used in the following patients only if no suitable treatment alternatives are available: those aged 65 years or above, those at increased risk of major cardiovascular problems (such as heart attack or stroke), those who smoke or have done so for a long time in the past and those at increased risk of cancer. … EMA has now concluded that these safety findings apply to all approved uses of JAK inhibitors in chronic inflammatory disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, axial spondyloarthritis, ulcerative colitis, atopic dermatitis and alopecia areata).

substances.name: minoxidil
substances.statement: In the EU, topical minoxidil medicines are authorised nationally (no centrally authorised product was found); after an EU safety review (CMDh, June 2024) their product information warns of reversible excess hair growth in infants after skin contact with a caregiver's application site.
substances.quote: Amendments to the product information of the nationally authorised medicinal product(s) … Cases of hypertrichosis have been reported in infants following skin contact with minoxidil application sites of patients (caregivers) using topical minoxidil. Hypertrichosis was reversible, within months, when infants were no longer exposed to minoxidil.
substances.quoteEn: Amendments to the product information of the nationally authorised medicinal product(s) … Cases of hypertrichosis have been reported in infants following skin contact with minoxidil application sites of patients (caregivers) using topical minoxidil. Hypertrichosis was reversible, within months, when infants were no longer exposed to minoxidil.

substances.name: minoxidil

substances.quote: cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … 6-(Piperidinyl)-2,4-pyrimidinediamine 3-oxide (Minoxidil (INN)) and its salts

substances.name: finasteride
substances.statement: In the EU, finasteride 1 mg tablets and a finasteride skin spray are authorised nationally in various member states for early androgenetic alopecia in men aged 18 to 41 (EMA, 2025).
substances.quote: Medicines containing finasteride 1 mg tablets or sprays to be applied to the skin are authorised in various EU Member States to prevent hair loss and stimulate hair growth in men aged 18 to 41 years with early-stage androgenetic alopecia (hair loss due to male hormones).
substances.quoteEn: Medicines containing finasteride 1 mg tablets or sprays to be applied to the skin are authorised in various EU Member States to prevent hair loss and stimulate hair growth in men aged 18 to 41 years with early-stage androgenetic alopecia (hair loss due to male hormones).

substances.name: finasteride
substances.statement: After an EU-wide review endorsed by the CMDh on 19 June 2025, suicidal ideation is a confirmed side effect of finasteride tablets; people taking 1 mg for hair loss who notice mood changes should stop and seek advice, and packs carry a patient card.
substances.quote: On 19 June 2025, the CMDh … Suicidal ideation was confirmed as a side effect of finasteride 1 and 5 mg tablets by the PRAC, following an EU-wide review of available data on these medicines. … A patient card will be included in the packages of 1 mg finasteride tablets to remind patients of these risks and to advise them about the appropriate course of action. … If you are taking finasteride 1 mg tablets for hair loss and you experience any mood changes, stop taking finasteride and contact your doctor for further medical advice as soon as possible.
substances.quoteEn: On 19 June 2025, the CMDh … Suicidal ideation was confirmed as a side effect of finasteride 1 and 5 mg tablets by the PRAC, following an EU-wide review of available data on these medicines. … A patient card will be included in the packages of 1 mg finasteride tablets to remind patients of these risks and to advise them about the appropriate course of action. … If you are taking finasteride 1 mg tablets for hair loss and you experience any mood changes, stop taking finasteride and contact your doctor for further medical advice as soon as possible.

substances.name: somatropin (growth hormone)
substances.statement: In the EU, somatropin is an injectable medicine authorised since the 1980s through central and national procedures for growth hormone replacement and for short stature in specific childhood conditions (EMA, 2012).
substances.quote: Medicines containing somatropin are given by injection. They have been authorised in the EU since the 1980s through centralised or national procedures … The approved indications vary for the different somatropin-containing medicines: they may be used as hormone replacement therapy, and to correct short stature (height) in children with certain genetic diseases (Turner syndrome or Prader Willi syndrome), children who have long-standing kidney problems and children born small for their gestational age.
substances.quoteEn: Medicines containing somatropin are given by injection. frameworks.statement: In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formula) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC, so they need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).
frameworks.quote: This Directive shall not apply to: … Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula). … Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula).
frameworks.quoteEn: This Directive shall not apply to: … Any medicinal product prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with a medical prescription for an individual patient (commonly known as the magistral formula). … Any medicinal product which is prepared in a pharmacy in accordance with the prescriptions of a pharmacopoeia and is intended to be supplied directly to the patients served by the pharmacy in question (commonly known as the officinal formula).

frameworks.statement: EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation that all other manufacture needs (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).
frameworks.quote: However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes.
frameworks.quoteEn: However, such authorization shall not be required for preparation, dividing up, changes in packaging or presentation where these processes are carried out, solely for retail supply, by pharmacists in dispensing pharmacies or by persons legally authorized in the Member States to carry out such processes.

frameworks.statement: In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)).
frameworks.quote: No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by the competent authorities of that Member State in accordance with this Directive or an authorisation has been granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004
frameworks.quoteEn: No medicinal product may be placed on the market of a Member State unless a marketing authorisation has been issued by the competent authorities of that Member State in accordance with this Directive or an authorisation has been granted in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 726/2004

frameworks.statement: EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).
frameworks.quote: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.
frameworks.quoteEn: A Member State may, in accordance with legislation in force and to fulfil special needs, exclude from the provisions of this Directive medicinal products supplied in response to a bona fide unsolicited order, formulated in accordance with the specifications of an authorised health-care professional and for use by an individual patient under his direct personal responsibility.

frameworks.statement: EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers in June 2024 to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses and said these medicines are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.
frameworks.quote: The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems.
frameworks.quoteEn: The MSSG therefore recommends that healthcare professionals prescribe these medicines in line with their authorised use(s) only, taking into account guidance issued by national authorities or applicable national therapeutic guidelines. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss, i.e. use for weight loss in people without obesity or people with overweight who do not have weight-related health problems.

frameworks.statement: Under EU law a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)).
frameworks.quote: Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or … Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis. … In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.
frameworks.quoteEn: Any substance or combination of substances presented as having properties for treating or preventing disease in human beings; or … Any substance or combination of substances which may be used in or administered to human beings either with a view to restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action, or to making a medical diagnosis. … In cases of doubt, where, taking into account all its characteristics, a product may fall within the definition of a ‘medicinal product’ and within the definition of a product covered by other Community legislation the provisions of this Directive shall apply.

frameworks.statement: The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).

frameworks.quoteEn: Medicinal products intended for research and development trials, but without prejudice to the provisions of Directive 2001/20/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 April 2001 on the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the Member States relating to the implementation of good clinical practice in the conduct of clinical trials on medicinal products for human use

frameworks.statement: Under EU law (Article 85c of Directive 2001/83/EC, inserted by the Falsified Medicines Directive 2011/62/EU), an online seller of medicines must be authorised in its member state, the medicines must comply with the law of the destination country, and the EU common logo must appear on every relevant page; member states may still ban online sale of prescription medicines.
frameworks.quote: Without prejudice to national legislation prohibiting the offer for sale at a distance of prescription medicinal products to the public by means of information society services … the natural or legal person offering the medicinal products is authorised or entitled to supply medicinal products to the public, also at a distance, in accordance with national legislation of the Member State in which that person is established … the medicinal products comply with the national legislation of the Member State of destination in accordance with Article 6(1) … the common logo referred to in paragraph 3 clearly displayed on every page of the website that relates to the offer for sale at a distance to the public of medicinal products
frameworks.quoteEn: Without prejudice to national legislation prohibiting the offer for sale at a distance of prescription medicinal products to the public by means of information society services … the natural or legal person offering the medicinal products is authorised or entitled to supply medicinal products to the public, also at a distance, in accordance with national legislation of the Member State in which that person is established … the medicinal products comply with the national legislation of the Member State of destination in accordance with Article 6(1) … the common logo referred to in paragraph 3 clearly displayed on every page of the website that relates to the offer for sale at a distance to the public of medicinal products

frameworks.statement: Since 1 July 2015 every legally operating online pharmacy or retailer in the EU should display the common logo (Implementing Regulation (EU) No 699/2014), which links to the national register; a logo showing the EU flag is not legal (European Commission).

As of 1st of July 2015, all online pharmacies or retailers legally operating in the EU should display the logo. … Therefore, a logo displaying the EU flag, for example, would not be legal.

As of 1st of July 2015, all online pharmacies or retailers legally operating in the EU should display the logo. … Therefore, a logo displaying the EU flag, for example, would not be legal.

frameworks.statement: EMA advises the public to buy medicines online only from retailers registered with national authorities, and to click the common logo and confirm the retailer is on the national register before buying.

These products, often sold via fraudulent websites and promoted on social media, are not authorised and do not meet necessary standards of quality, safety and efficacy. … They may not contain the claimed active substance at all and may contain harmful levels of other substances.

frameworks.statement: In the EU, a cosmetic is a substance or mixture placed on the external parts of the body (skin, hair, nails, lips, external genitals) or teeth and oral mucosa, mainly to clean, perfume, change appearance, protect, keep in good condition or correct body odour (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(1)(a)).
frameworks.quote: ‘cosmetic product’ means any substance or mixture intended to be placed in contact with the external parts of the human body (epidermis, hair system, nails, lips and external genital organs) or with the teeth and the mucous membranes of the oral cavity with a view exclusively or mainly to cleaning them, perfuming them, changing their appearance, protecting them, keeping them in good condition or correcting body odours

frameworks.statement: In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)), so an injected peptide can never be a cosmetic.

frameworks.statement: The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in 5.5) says a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic, and one sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.
frameworks.quote: If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation … Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis
frameworks.quoteEn: If a substance or mixture presented in a vial or ampoule is for use by injection, then the product cannot be considered to meet the definition of a cosmetic product by virtue of Article 2(2) of the Cosmetics Regulation … Furthermore, the product should not be marketed with a device which could allow the injection of this product or its delivery below the epidermis

frameworks.statement: The EU borderline manual says products used with needle rollers are cosmetics only if the product stays in the epidermis; if the needles reach the dermis, the product cannot be a cosmetic.
frameworks.quote: If the use of the roller only ena bles the application of the product in the epidermis, then the product is a cosmetic and its safety should be assessed taking into account the composition and the mode of delivery. On the other hand, if the needles reach the dermis, the use of the roller induces a deeper application of the product, and therefore this product cannot be qualified as a cosmetic.
frameworks.quoteEn: If the use of the roller only ena bles the application of the product in the epidermis, then the product is a cosmetic and its safety should be assessed taking into account the composition and the mode of delivery. On the other hand, if the needles reach the dermis, the use of the roller induces a deeper application of the product, and therefore this product cannot be qualified as a cosmetic.

frameworks.statement: Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities; the borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic (June 2025).
frameworks.quote: However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics. … A decision on the qualification of the products has to be made by the na tional competent authorities on a case -by-case basis
frameworks.quoteEn: However, some products presented as anti -wrinkle may significantly restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action. In that case, they would not qualify as cosmetics. … A decision on the qualification of the products has to be made by the na tional competent authorities on a case -by-case basis

frameworks.statement: The EU borderline manual notes that a product can act pharmacologically, and so fall outside cosmetics law, even when its ingredient is not used in any medicine, naming 'some specially designed peptides' in eyelash-growth products.
frameworks.quote: other substances with an influence on eyelash growth may exist (or be designed), which are not used as active drug ingredients, but the product containing them could still restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (e.g. some specially designed peptides).
frameworks.quoteEn: other substances with an influence on eyelash growth may exist (or be designed), which are not used as active drug ingredients, but the product containing them could still restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action (e.g. some specially designed peptides).

frameworks.statement: The EU borderline manual states that topical products working through hormones or hormone-like substances (its example: breast-augmentation products) act pharmacologically and cannot be cosmetics.
frameworks.quote: Topical breast augmentation products achieve their objective through the action of hormones … They therefore significantly " restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action " … and cannot be qualified as cosmetic products.
frameworks.quoteEn: Topical breast augmentation products achieve their objective through the action of hormones … They therefore significantly " restore, correct or modify physiological functions by exerting a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action " … and cannot be qualified as cosmetic products.

frameworks.statement: EU cosmetics law also prohibits substances with androgenic effect and steroidal anti-androgens in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II entries 37 and 390).
frameworks.quote: cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Substances with androgenic effect … Anti-androgens of steroidal structure
frameworks.quoteEn: cosmetic products shall not contain any of the following: … prohibited substances listed in Annex II … Substances with androgenic effect … Anti-androgens of steroidal structure

frameworks.statement: Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market it needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a cosmetic product safety report, and electronic notification to the Commission (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Articles 4, 10 and 13).
frameworks.quote: Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market. … the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I. … Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission
frameworks.quoteEn: Only cosmetic products for which a legal or natural person is designated within the Community as ‘responsible person’ shall be placed on the market. … the responsible person shall, prior to placing a cosmetic product on the market, ensure that the cosmetic product has undergone a safety assessment on the basis of the relevant information and that a cosmetic product safety report is set up in accordance with Annex I. … Prior to placing the cosmetic product on the market the responsible person shall submit, by electronic means, the following information to the Commission

frameworks.statement: In the EU, cosmetic labelling, marketing and advertising must not use text, names, pictures or signs implying that a product has characteristics or functions it does not have (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 20(1)).
frameworks.quote: In the labelling, making available on the market and advertising of cosmetic products, text, names, trade marks, pictures and figurative or other signs shall not be used to imply that these products have characteristics or functions which they do not have.
frameworks.quoteEn: In the labelling, making available on the market and advertising of cosmetic products, text, names, trade marks, pictures and figurative or other signs shall not be used to imply that these products have characteristics or functions which they do not have.

frameworks.statement: EU cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and a claim that extrapolates an ingredient's properties (for example a peptide's) to the finished product needs evidence such as the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013).
frameworks.quote: Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments. … A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.
frameworks.quoteEn: Claims for cosmetic products, whether explicit or implicit, shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence regardless of the types of evidential support used to substantiate them, including where appropriate expert assessments. … A claim extrapolating (explicitly or implicitly) ingredient properties to the finished product shall be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, such as by demonstrating the presence of the ingredient at an effective concentration.

frameworks.statement: The Commission's CosIng database is not legally binding: a listing does not determine an ingredient's regulatory status, which only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes set (read 25 September 2026).
frameworks.quote: CosIng is a non-legally binding information database. It provides information on cosmetic ingredients but does not, in itself, determine their regulatory status. Only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes establish whether, and under which conditions, substances may be used in cosmetic products.
frameworks.quoteEn: CosIng is a non-legally binding information database. It provides information on cosmetic ingredients but does not, in itself, determine their regulatory status. Only Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its Annexes establish whether, and under which conditions, substances may be used in cosmetic products.

frameworks.statement: Injectable dermal fillers without a medical purpose are regulated in the EU under the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 as Annex XVI products.
frameworks.quote: LIST OF GROUPS OF PRODUCTS WITHOUT AN INTENDED MEDICAL PURPOSE REFERRED TO IN ARTICLE 1(2) … Substances, combinations of substances, or items intended to be used for facial or other dermal or mucous membrane filling by subcutaneous, submucous or intradermal injection or other introduction, excluding those for tattooing.
frameworks.quoteEn: LIST OF GROUPS OF PRODUCTS WITHOUT AN INTENDED MEDICAL PURPOSE REFERRED TO IN ARTICLE 1(2) … Substances, combinations of substances, or items intended to be used for facial or other dermal or mucous membrane filling by subcutaneous, submucous or intradermal injection or other introduction, excluding those for tattooing.

frameworks.statement: In the EU, food supplements are foods that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are sold in measured doses such as capsules, tablets or sachets (Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a)).
frameworks.quote: ‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder, ampoules of liquids, drop dispensing bottles, and other similar forms of liquids and powders designed to be taken in measured small unit quantities
frameworks.quoteEn: ‘food supplements’ means foodstuffs the purpose of which is to supplement the normal diet and which are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, alone or in combination, marketed in dose form, namely forms such as capsules, pastilles, tablets, pills and other similar forms, sachets of powder, ampoules of liquids, drop dispensing bottles, and other similar forms of liquids and powders designed to be taken in measured small unit quantities

frameworks.statement: In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).
frameworks.quote: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.
frameworks.quoteEn: Health claims shall be prohibited unless they comply with the general requirements in Chapter II and the specific requirements in this Chapter and are authorised in accordance with this Regulation and included in the lists of authorised claims provided for in Articles 13 and 14.

frameworks.statement: The EU authorised claim linking collagen to skin is a vitamin C claim — 'Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin' — usable only on foods that are at least a source of vitamin C (Regulation (EU) No 432/2012).
frameworks.quote: Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin … The claim may be used only for food which is at least a source of vitamin C as referred to in the claim SOURCE OF [NAME OF VITAMIN/S] AND/OR [NAME OF MINERAL/S] as listed in the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
frameworks.quoteEn: Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation for the normal function of skin … The claim may be used only for food which is at least a source of vitamin C as referred to in the claim SOURCE OF [NAME OF VITAMIN/S] AND/OR [NAME OF MINERAL/S] as listed in the Annex to Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.

frameworks.statement: In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4)).
frameworks.quote: food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties. … Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall also apply to: … advertising
frameworks.quoteEn: food information shall not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, nor refer to such properties. … Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall also apply to: … advertising

frameworks.statement: In the EU, a food not consumed to a significant degree in the Union before 15 May 1997 (for example, one with a new molecular structure) is a novel food and may be sold only once authorised and listed in the Union list (Regulation (EU) 2015/2283, Articles 3 and 6).
frameworks.quote: ‘novel food’ means any food that was not used for human consumption to a significant degree within the Union before 15 May 1997 … food with a new or intentionally modified molecular structure, where that structure was not used as, or in, a food within the Union before 15 May 1997 … Only novel foods authorised and included in the Union list may be placed on the market within the Union as such, or used in or on foods
frameworks.quoteEn: ‘novel food’ means any food that was not used for human consumption to a significant degree within the Union before 15 May 1997 … food with a new or intentionally modified molecular structure, where that structure was not used as, or in, a food within the Union before 15 May 1997 … Only novel foods authorised and included in the Union list may be placed on the market within the Union as such, or used in or on foods

frameworks.statement: EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 87).
frameworks.quote: Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law. … All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics.
frameworks.quoteEn: Member States shall prohibit any advertising of a medicinal product in respect of which a marketing authorization has not been granted in accordance with Community law. … All parts of the advertising of a medicinal product must comply with the particulars listed in the summary of product characteristics.

frameworks.statement: EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)); 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Article 86(1)).
frameworks.quote: ‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products … Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which: … are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI
frameworks.quoteEn: ‘advertising of medicinal products’ shall include any form of door-to-door information, canvassing activity or inducement designed to promote the prescription, supply, sale or consumption of medicinal products … Member States shall prohibit the advertising to the general public of medicinal products which: … are available on medical prescription only, in accordance with Title VI

frameworks.statement: Where EU law allows advertising of a medicine to the public, it must not refer to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or celebrities, or suggest the medicine is a cosmetic (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 90).
frameworks.quote: The advertising of a medicinal product to the general public shall not contain any material which: … refers to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or persons who are neither of the foregoing but who, because of their celebrity, could encourage the consumption of medicinal products … suggests that the medicinal product is a foodstuff, cosmetic or other consumer product
frameworks.quoteEn: The advertising of a medicinal product to the general public shall not contain any material which: … refers to a recommendation by scientists, health professionals or persons who are neither of the foregoing but who, because of their celebrity, could encourage the consumption of medicinal products … suggests that the medicinal product is a foodstuff, cosmetic or other consumer product

frameworks.statement: When medicines are promoted to prescribers or suppliers in the EU, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be offered unless inexpensive and relevant to practice, and prescribers must not solicit or accept prohibited inducements (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 94).
frameworks.quote: Where medicinal products are being promoted to persons qualified to prescribe or supply them, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be supplied, offered or promised to such persons unless they are inexpensive and relevant to the practice of medicine or pharmacy. … Persons qualified to prescribe or supply medicinal products shall not solicit or accept any inducement prohibited under paragraph 1 or contrary to paragraph 2.
frameworks.quoteEn: Where medicinal products are being promoted to persons qualified to prescribe or supply them, no gifts, pecuniary advantages or benefits in kind may be supplied, offered or promised to such persons unless they are inexpensive and relevant to the practice of medicine or pharmacy. … Persons qualified to prescribe or supply medicinal products shall not solicit or accept any inducement prohibited under paragraph 1 or contrary to paragraph 2.

frameworks.statement: EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must take measures to apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Articles 9(1)(f) and 28b(2)).
frameworks.quote: audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatment available only on prescription in the Member State within whose jurisdiction the media service provider falls shall be prohibited … Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers
frameworks.quoteEn: audiovisual commercial communications for medicinal products and medical treatment available only on prescription in the Member State within whose jurisdiction the media service provider falls shall be prohibited … Member States shall ensure that the video-sharing platform providers under their jurisdiction take appropriate measures to comply with the requirements set out in Article 9(1) with respect to audiovisual commercial communications that are not marketed, sold or arranged by those video-sharing platform providers

frameworks.statement: EU consumer law blacklists falsely claiming that a product can cure illnesses, dysfunction or malformations as an unfair commercial practice in all circumstances (Directive 2005/29/EC, Annex I point 17).
frameworks.quote: Falsely claiming that a product is able to cure illnesses, dysfunction or malformations.
frameworks.quoteEn: Falsely claiming that a product is able to cure illnesses, dysfunction or malformations.

frameworks.statement: EU criminal drug-trafficking law defines 'drug' as substances covered by the UN 1961 and 1971 conventions plus the new psychoactive substances listed in its Annex; none of the course substances appears in that Annex (Framework Decision 2004/757/JHA, consolidated 12 January 2026), so controlled status is set by national and UN schedules.
frameworks.quote: ‘drug’: means any of the following: … a substance covered by the 1961 United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, as amended by the 1972 Protocol, or by the 1971 United Nations Convention on Psychotropic Substances; … any of the substances listed in the Annex
frameworks.quoteEn: ‘drug’: means any of the following: … a substance covered by the 1961 United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, as amended by the 1972 Protocol, or by the 1971 United Nations Convention on Psychotropic Substances; … any of the substances listed in the Annex

frameworks.statement: EU marketing authorisations can restrict who prescribes: Scenesse (afamelanotide) is prescribed only by specialist doctors in recognised EPP centres and used only by properly trained doctors (EMA).
frameworks.quote: Scenesse is only prescribed by specialist doctors in recognised centres for treating EPP and should only be used by doctors who have been properly trained.
frameworks.quoteEn: Scenesse is only prescribed by specialist doctors in recognised centres for treating EPP and should only be used by doctors who have been properly trained.

authorFindings: Directive 2001/83/EC is still the EU medicines code: EUR-Lex shows the 1 January 2025 consolidation as current with no end date. Its replacement (the 'Union code', procedure 2023/0132 (COD)) was politically agreed and, per Council note 12263/26 of 21 September 2026, awaits the Council's first-reading position and Parliament's second reading (eu-council-st-12263-2026). Re-check before publishing, and date every EU statement.

The EU has no counterpart to US 503A/503B compounding categories: magistral and officinal preparations sit outside Directive 2001/83/EC (Article 3) and pharmacy preparation is exempt from manufacturing authorisation (Article 40(2)), so the rules on what a pharmacy may compound, and from which active substances, are national. Do not map FDA category lists onto EU learners.

The EU line for peptide skin products runs through three instruments: a topical product with a cosmetic purpose is a cosmetic (1223/2009); anything injected or implanted is never a cosmetic (Art 2(2)), nor is a vial product sold with an injecting device or a needle-roller product reaching the dermis (borderline manual); an injected product without a medical purpose may be a device (MDR Annex XVI fillers), and anything acting pharmacologically is a medicine (2001/83 Art 1(2), with Art 2(2) resolving doubt towards medicines law).

Several substances in the course are banned from EU cosmetics outright: tretinoin (Annex II/375), minoxidil (II/372), oestrogens (II/260), progestogens (II/194), substances with androgenic effect (II/37) and steroidal anti-androgens (II/390). A 'cosmeceutical' containing them is an illegal cosmetic, whatever its label says.

Collagen marketing: the EU refused a VeriSol®P collagen-peptide claim on skin elasticity and wrinkles (Regulation 1154/2014) and the general 'collagen helps skin firmness and elasticity' claim is non-authorised in the EU Register (POL-HC-8291). The only authorised claim that mentions skin collagen is the vitamin C claim, which explains why EU collagen supplements often add vitamin C.

Orphan designations are not authorisations but appear in marketing: ibutamoren mesilate (MK-677) holds EU/3/17/1882 for growth hormone deficiency (2017), and afamelanotide holds designations beyond EPP (e.g. xeroderma pigmentosum and variegate porphyria, 2024, per EMA's orphan-designation table read 25 September 2026).

EMA's medicines table (25 September 2026) also lists items the course may want: Litfulo (ritlecitinib), a second JAK inhibitor, centrally authorised on 15 September 2023 and indicated for severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over (EMA data table); long-acting growth hormones Sogroya (somapacitan, 2021), Ngenla (somatrogon, 2022) and Skytrofa (lonapegsomatropin, 2022); and Kayshild (semaglutide, 2026) for MASH. Verify indications from the EPARs before using them.

Safety updates EU clinicians should know: semaglutide — NAION very rare side effect (PRAC, June 2025); finasteride — suicidal ideation confirmed, patient card (2025); topical minoxidil — infant hypertrichosis warning (2024); JAK inhibitors — restricted use in higher-risk groups (2023); topical retinoids — not in pregnancy (2018).

The June 2024 EMA/HMA call not to use GLP-1 receptor agonists for cosmetic weight loss was issued during shortages; EMA's shortage table now marks the Ozempic shortage resolved (last updated 13 January 2026), but the statement that these medicines are not approved for cosmetic weight loss remains true of their authorised indications.

Europol's SHIELD VI summary (25 February 2026) describes a Spanish network supplying illegal medicines and health products for cosmetic medicine to legal and clandestine clinics, with activity extending to Portugal — useful context for the PT file.

Method note: EUR-Lex answers automated requests with an empty 202 (bot protection), so every EU legal text was read from the Publications Office (Cellar) copy of the same document; the source URLs point there so the claim-support fetcher can read them, and each note gives the EUR-Lex link for learners. CosIng, the EU claims register screen and Europol are JavaScript pages read in a browser.
